The flight. A narrow-body airliner arriving at an airport for a visual approach. Clear weather with good visibility.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring.

What happened. On the downwind leg the crew were cleared for a visual approach, with the satellite (RNAV) approach to the same runway loaded in the flight management system as a backup. The captain planned to turn onto base and join the final approach course at or outside the final approach fix, which has a published altitude of 2,900 ft. To check that altitude, the captain looked at the approach chart and read the altitude for a different fix, 2,160 ft. At the captain's request the flight plan was sequenced to that fix. The captain set 2,100 ft in the altitude selector and began a descent on the downwind leg. At the same time the captain began slowing the aircraft to start configuring for landing, so the descent was fairly slow. Descending through about 2,300 ft, the captain saw that the aircraft appeared to be getting low, looked again at the chart, and saw that the altitude selected belonged to the other fix. At about the same time, as the aircraft neared 2,100 ft, the landing gear not down warning sounded and the tower issued a low altitude alert, which the first officer acknowledged. The captain immediately began a climb to about 3,000 ft.

The approach was stable throughout and the aircraft landed without further incident. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.

The flight. A wide-body airliner departing from an airport in the early hours of the morning. Visual conditions, with wind.

The crew. The first officer was the pilot flying for the take-off and the captain the pilot monitoring. The captain taxied and lined up the aircraft. A relief first officer was also on the flight deck.

What happened. The crew had completed the before-take-off checklist and runway verification. The captain noted several aircraft on final. The taxiway from the holding point joins the runway in a curve. As a landing aircraft crossed the threshold, the tower controller cleared this aircraft to line up and wait. The landing aircraft reported that it had passed its planned exit, and the controller told it to expedite to the next one. The controller then cleared this aircraft for an immediate take-off. It was still taxiing into position, in a slight right turn onto the centreline. The captain centred the nose on the centreline while continuing to roll forward, as usual, and believed the line-up was complete. The captain asked whether everyone was ready, handed control to the first officer, set 55 per cent thrust and, when stable, selected take-off thrust. The main gear trucks had not yet locked into position after the turn. A take-off configuration warning sounded, with a main gear steering message. At about 10 knots the captain rejected the take-off and took control. The first officer told the tower that they had rejected the take-off on the runway.

The flight. An airliner on a passenger flight to an airport in mountainous terrain, in daylight and visual conditions.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring.

What happened. After runway and approach changes and a hold, ATC vectored the aircraft to the approach with a turn of more than 90 degrees; it overshot the inbound course and S-turned onto final. At 1,000 ft the approach was stable: configured, on path, on the 152-knot target speed, runway in sight. At about 500 ft the airspeed rose about 15 knots. The captain reduced power; the speed stayed at 160 knots and the PAPI showed slightly high. Lowering the nose brought a "Sink rate" warning; the captain corrected, reduced power again and lowered the nose slightly, and a second warning sounded. Holding power, in case the added headwind was lost, the captain raised the nose and moved the aim point to 1,500 ft. The manual required a go-around for a sink-rate warning at or below 500 ft unless, in visual conditions, the captain judged the deviation was being corrected immediately and safely. The captain judged that it was, and that the approach was still stable. The captain knew the runway's initial downslope would partly offset the higher descent rate, and saw risk in a go-around in mountainous terrain, with a controller who seemed to be having difficulty managing arrivals. Judging it safer to continue to a controlled touchdown-zone landing, the captain continued.
